info.title: Landbot Bots API v0-alpha
info.description:
Create a bot, edit its draft block by block, test it, publish it.

New here? Read **[How a bot works](https://dev.landbot.io/api-reference/bots/concepts)** first —
the draft, the diagram, and what an answer looks like.
**[When a call fails](https://dev.landbot.io/api-reference/bots/errors)** has every status and
every rule a diagram can break.

Two operations below are described and not built yet. Each says so, and says what a request to it
answers today.

servers.description: Same-origin, as consumed by the builder

tags.name: Bots
tags.description: The bot, its settings and its lifecycle

tags.name: Catalog
tags.description: The blocks available to place in a diagram

tags.name: Connected accounts
tags.description: The accounts a brand connected, as a block names them

get.description:
A page of your bots, newest publication first. `order` also takes `-created_at` and `name`.

`state=trashed` lists what is in the trash instead of what is in use.

Sorting by when the content last changed is not offered.

parameters.name: search
parameters.description: Case-insensitive match on the bot name

parameters.name: channel_family
parameters.description: The family the bot runs on. Filtering by channel type is not offered.

post.description:
Creates the bot, its draft, its test copy and — for a `landbot` bot — a web channel.

Without `diagram` the draft holds a start point and nothing else. With one, the bot can be
talked to straight away; a diagram that breaks a rule is refused and nothing is created.

`source` duplicates a bot. Not built yet: `501`.

404.description:
The bot given as `source` does not exist. Reached only once `source` is served; today a
`source` is refused with `501`, so a creation never answers `404`.

422.description:
Nothing was created — no bot, no test copy, no channel. Every refusal carries a `code`:
an unknown `channel_family`, a `workspace` that is not yours, a `name` over 50
characters, or `diagram` and `source` together.

A `diagram` that breaks the rules also lists them in `violations`.

get.description:
Settings and lifecycle state. No diagram — read `GET /bots/{bot_id}/draft` for the one you are
editing, or a version for a published one.

patch.summary: Update settings, or restore from trash
patch.description:
Writes only the fields you send. An empty body answers `400`, and so does a field we do not
describe.

**`state: active` is how you take a bot out of the trash**, and the only value `state` accepts. Any
other write to a trashed bot answers `404`, as if it were not there.

delete.summary: Move a bot to the trash, or delete it permanently
delete.description:
Moves the bot to the trash. It stops serving conversations and a web bot's page comes down, but
nothing is destroyed: `PATCH` with `state: active` brings it back whole.

`?permanent=true` destroys it, versions and all. Only works on a bot already in the trash, and cannot
be undone.

parameters.name: permanent
parameters.description: Delete irreversibly instead of moving to the trash

422.description: Permanent deletion was requested for a bot that is not in the trash

get.description:
Whether the bot asks how the conversation went, and the wording it uses.

A bot nobody has configured answers `enabled: false` and the wording it would use.

put.description:
Replaces the whole configuration. Only `enabled` is required, and **any wording you leave out goes
back to the default** rather than staying as it was.

The change reaches conversations the bot is already having.

200.description: The feedback configuration after the change

get.description:
The diagram you are editing, its save state, and the violations the last write recorded.

Those are the last write's verdict, not a fresh one. Publishing checks again and can refuse a draft
this reports as clean.

put.description:
Replaces the whole diagram. This is the autosave path, so **nothing is rejected**: a diagram that
breaks rules is stored anyway and comes back with `save_state` and `violations`. You never lose work,
and publishing is what refuses.

Kept as you sent it, keys and all. The one thing we add is `isTarget: true`, on any node that does
not already say whether a connection may end at it.

200.description: The stored draft, with the outcome of validating it

patch.summary: Apply a set of changes to the draft
patch.description:
Adds, updates and deletes blocks and connections in one go. All of it applies or none of it does.

Use this whenever a change spans more than one block — the single-block endpoints carry no
connections, so they cannot rewire.

**Describe the result you want, not the steps.** Every problem in the set is collected and answered
together. `removed_connections` lists the wiring that went.

200.description: The draft after the change set

422.description:
The set cannot be applied and nothing was written: everything it breaks is listed in
`violations`. A bot a previous builder built is refused here too, and carries no
`violations`.

delete.description:
**Not built yet.** The path is served for other methods, so your credentials are checked and then
the method is refused: you get `405`.

Would reset the draft to the published version, discarding unpublished work.

405.description:
The method is not served yet. Carries `detail`, and this is what the operation answers
today.

422.description: The bot has never been published, so there is nothing to reset to

post.description:
Adds blocks, with their connections, to the diagram you already have. All of them apply or none do.
`top` and `left` say where on the canvas each one goes.

Broken rules are stored and reported, as on autosave. A few problems are refused outright instead —
[When a call fails](https://dev.landbot.io/api-reference/bots/errors) lists which.

This only adds. To change or remove something, use `PATCH /bots/{bot_id}/draft`.

patch.description:
Changes one block. **`params` is replaced whole**, so send the ones you want kept; anything you omit
falls back to its default. Params we do not describe are left alone. `top` and `left` move it on the
canvas; omit them and it stays where it was drawn.

This endpoint carries no connections, so removing a button or an exit that a connection leaves from is
refused. Use `PATCH /bots/{bot_id}/draft` to do both at once.

404.description: The bot or the block does not exist

delete.description:
Removes the block and every connection touching it, in either direction. They come back in
`removed_connections`.

Delete the block the bot starts from and the draft breaks `start_connection` until something fills the
slot. That is how you replace a greeting: delete, then add.

404.description: The bot or the block does not exist

get.description:
**Not built yet.** There is no such path, so you get a `404` as an HTML page, credentials or not.

Would be a rolling history of draft states, to step back an edit without a full reset.

200.description: A page of revisions, most recent first

put.description:
Puts the current draft on the bot's test channel so you can talk to it. Writing the draft
does not do this.

**Any violation stops the deployment**, not only the ones that stop a publication.

To talk to it you need that channel's configuration, from the
[Channels API](https://dev.landbot.io/api-reference/channels-api).

200.description: The draft is deployed and ready to be exercised

422.description:
The draft breaks business rules and was not deployed, or a previous builder built the bot
and it was not written at all — the second carries no `violations`.

get.description:
A page of the bot's publications, newest first: when, who, and the label if it has one. No diagrams —
read a single version for that.

A bot nobody has published answers an empty page, not a `404`.

200.description: A page of versions, most recent first

post.description:
**Publishing is creating a version.** Sent empty, it checks the draft and puts it live. Any violation
refuses it.

Sent with `source`, it restores that version: the diagram goes back into your draft and is published
from there, so the history only ever grows.

Answers the publication, not the version — no id and no `Location` header yet.

404.description:
`bot_not_found` when there is no such bot, or it is not yours — the two answer alike.
`version_not_found` when the `source` names a version this bot never published.

422.description:
The draft breaks rules, listed in `violations`. Three different codes:

- `draft_has_violations` — publishing the draft. Nothing changed.
- `restored_draft_has_violations` — restoring. **The version is already in your draft**,
  so this one is not a no-op: fix it there and publish again.
- `version_of_an_unsupported_builder` — the version was written by an older builder and
  cannot be brought back. Nothing changed.

get.description:
The bot's last publication, answered like any other version.

A bot that has never published answers `404` — never the draft in its place.

404.description:
The bot has never been published, or there is no such bot to read — it does not exist,
or it is not the caller's. The three are answered alike, down to the `code`, so nothing
here says which it was. See `NotFound` for why another brand's bot answers this.

get.description:
One publication: the diagram as it went out, and a snapshot of the channel it went out on.

To bring it back, publish it — `POST /bots/{bot_id}/versions` with this version as `source`.

404.description:
There is nothing to read: no version of that id was published for the bot, or there is
no such bot — it does not exist, or it is not the caller's. All of them are answered
alike, down to the `code`, so nothing here says which it was. See `NotFound` for why
another brand's bot answers this.

patch.description:
The label is the only thing about a version you can change. `name` is required; send `null` to take a
label off. An empty string is refused.

Answers the publication without its diagram. Nothing the bot is serving changes.

delete.description:
Removes the publication from the history, and with it the diagram and the channel snapshot it filed.
Cannot be undone. Does not touch what is live.

**The most recent publication cannot be deleted.** Publish again and it becomes deletable.

422.description:
The version is the bot's most recent publication, and nothing was deleted, under the code
`version_is_the_most_recent_publication`. A version the caller cannot read answers `404`
instead, whichever of the two it is.

get.description:
This contract, as YAML, from the environment you are calling. Use it to check what that environment
answers rather than trusting a copy.

Needs the permission to view bots, like any other read here.

Every block you can place in a diagram: its params and rules, outputs, defaults, the plan tier
it needs and the channels it runs on.

A block whose behaviour changes with a param is described as variants; `selector` says which
params pick each.

The catalogue grows a family at a time, so a diagram may hold blocks it does not cover.

parameters.name: channel_family
parameters.description:
Restrict to blocks available on a channel family. Not served yet: it is accepted and
ignored, and the whole catalog comes back.

get.summary: The Google accounts connected to the brand
get.description:
The accounts a `google_spreadsheets` block can go through, numbered the way its `auth_id`
takes them. Each one is a Google account somebody connected to the brand. Connecting one is
a consent a person gives at Google in the browser, and this API starts it:
`POST /connected-accounts/google_spreadsheets/connections` answers a link a member of the
brand opens in the app, and `GET .../connections/{id}` says when the account is connected and
which one it is. So an empty list is answered by starting a connection and handing the link
to a person in the brand, not by anything a token does on its own.

Two kinds of account are not listed, because the builder offers them nowhere: one that was
revoked, and one connected with the scopes the app no longer accepts, which the app asks to be
reconnected. Connecting the same Google account again, in the app or through a connection,
makes it appear here with the id it already had.

What comes back is the id and the name. Never a token: the credential stays where it is.

What the block names below the account — the file, the tab and its columns — is read
through it by the operations below, with the same credential.

Needs the permission to view integrations, as the API the builder goes through does.

200.description: The accounts, most recently connected first

get.description:
The files the account can reach, as Google Drive identifies them, which is what a block's
`spreadsheet_id` takes.

The account's scope lists only the files the app created or the person picked in the
builder, so a file you know of is usually missing here: one made in Drive by hand, or one the
person's own Drive tooling created or found. Its id — the long segment of the file's URL
between `/d/` and `/edit` — is still valid for the block and for the two reads below, which
take any file the account can open in Drive.

Needs the permission to view integrations.

Each tab, with its title and its own id.

**`title` is what the block's `sheet_name` takes**, and the only one of the two that is
compiled. `id` is what the editor keeps to know which tab is selected: writing it where the
title goes leaves a block that fails when the bot runs.

Needs the permission to view integrations.

get.summary: The columns of a tab's header row
get.description:
The header row of the tab, one entry per column that has a header: its number counting from
1, which is what `selectorValue` takes in a block's `selectors` and `reference`, and what the
header says. A column with an empty header is skipped, so the numbers may have gaps.

Needs the permission to view integrations.

post.summary: Ask a person to connect a Google account
post.description:
Connecting an account is a consent Google asks a person for in the browser, and nothing a
token can do on its own. This starts one: it answers a `url` that a member of the brand
opens, signed in to the app, to see who asked and go through Google. When they finish, the
account is connected to the brand, and the connection below says which one it is.

The link lives fifteen minutes and is answered once. Hand it to a person in the brand who
may edit integrations: anyone else is refused at the page, and so is a link already
answered. Then poll the connection every few seconds; there is no push.

Takes no body. Needs the permission to edit integrations, as connecting an account in the
app does.

201.description: The connection, and where it is followed

get.description:
`pending` while nobody has answered. `connected` once the person consented: `account_id` is
then what a `google_spreadsheets` block's `auth_id` takes, and the account is listed from
then on. `declined` when the person cancelled at the page or Google refused. `expired` when
fifteen minutes passed with no answer. A connection is answered once: to try again, start
another.

Needs the permission to view integrations.

200.description: The connection as it stands right now

sessionCookie.name: sessionid
sessionCookie.description: Same-origin session, used by the builder

agentToken.name: Authorization
agentToken.description: An agent's own token, sent as `Token <value>`. This is how the public API is reached.

BlockId.name: block_id
BlockId.description: The block's id within the diagram

AccountId.name: account_id
AccountId.description:
The connected account, as `GET /connected-accounts/google_spreadsheets` numbers it and as a
block's `auth_id` names it.

SpreadsheetId.name: spreadsheet_id
SpreadsheetId.description: The file, as Google Drive identifies it.

SheetTitle.name: sheet_title
SheetTitle.description:
The tab's title, as `.../sheets` lists it under `title`. A title containing `/` cannot be
addressed here.

ConnectionId.name: connection_id
ConnectionId.description: The connection, as starting one answered it.

State.name: state
State.description: Lifecycle state. Defaults to `active`, so trashed bots are not listed.

Order.name: order
Order.description:
How the page is sorted. `-last_published_at` is the most recently published first,
`-created_at` the most recently created first, and `name` alphabetical.

BadRequest.description:
The request could not be read: a field missing, carrying the wrong type, or one this
operation does not write. Keyed by what is at fault, and `non_field_errors` for a problem
that belongs to no single field.

Unauthorized.description:
No credentials, or credentials that name nobody: none were sent, or the token is not a valid
one. Nobody was resolved, so there is no caller to be forbidden.

NoSuchPath.description:
There is no such path. The answer is an HTML page, not JSON, and your credentials are never
looked at.

TooManyRequests.description:
Too many requests. **Every call counts, reads included** — the limit is on how fast you call,
not on how much you change. It is 40 a second, counted per member rather than per account, so
two people generating at once each get their own.

NotFound.description:
No such bot, or not yours. The two answer identically, on every operation, whatever else may
be wrong with the bot.

NoSuchConnectedAccount.description:
No such connected account, or not yours, or revoked, or one the app asks to reconnect: the
listing leaves those out, and a read through one answers the same way. So does an account
whose credential Google refuses to renew on this very read, which revokes it. All answer
identically, with the code `connected_account_not_found`.

NoSuchConnection.description:
No such connection, or not yours. Both answer identically, with the code
`connection_not_found`. An answered or expired connection is still found: its status says so.

RuleViolated.description:
We understood you and refused. `violations` lists what broke, and which block, when the
rules point at one.

NotServedYet.description:
We understood you and have not built this yet. Nothing changed, and there is nothing to send
instead — the same request will work once it is built.

Duplicating a bot is the only request that answers this today.

DependencyFailure.description: Something we depend on failed. Nothing changed, so retrying is reasonable.

UnsupportedBot.description:
An older builder built this bot, and we write only our own. Reading it still works; writing
it needs it migrated first.

UnreadableChannelFamily.description:
The bot's channel family is missing or is one we do not recognise, so we cannot tell you
where it runs. We do not guess.

On a listing this refuses the whole page, not the one bot: a page that quietly dropped it
would be lying about how many bots you have.

BotState.description:
`active` is a bot in use. `trashed` is a bot that has been deleted but is recoverable; it
does not serve conversations.

PlanTier.description: A subscription tier, ordered from lowest to highest.

SaveState.description:
The outcome of the last write to the draft. `IS_PRESAVED` is a stored diagram with no
violations, `HAS_ERRORS` a stored diagram that broke at least one rule, `IS_VALIDATED` a
draft deployed for testing and `IS_PUBLISHED` one that has been published.

`HAS_ERRORS` is the one that matters: while the draft is in it, the bot cannot be published.

Timestamp.description:
A moment, in UTC, written as `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SS`. It carries no offset and no fraction of a
second, so a client that reads it as local time is wrong by whatever its own offset is.

total.description: Total number of items across all pages

FeedbackConfig.description:
What the bot asks at the end of a conversation.

A wording that is too long, empty or blank is refused rather than trimmed. An answer never
carries a blank one: you get the default instead.

thank_you_message.description: What the bot answers once the user has replied.

Bot.description:
A bot, as writing one and as reading one both report it. It carries everything a listing
item does, plus the two things only a single bot's answer knows — the channels it is reached
through and whether its draft carries changes — and minus who wrote each side, which a
caller looking at one bot has not asked for.

channels.description:
The channels that serve the bot. A web bot is created with one; a bot can be served by
more than one, and channels are managed outside this API.

state.description:
Whether the bot is in use or in the trash. Reported by reading a bot and by writing one
alike: the trash is a state of the bot, so a write knows which side of it the bot it
left behind is on.

is_active.description:
Whether the bot serves conversations. This is separate from `state`: a bot in the
`active` state can still be deactivated, and a trashed bot never serves regardless of
this flag.

preview_only.description:
The bot runs in preview only, because it needs a higher plan tier than the brand has, or
because the brand's subscription has lapsed. Derived on the subscription side and never
set through this API.

required_tier.description: The lowest plan tier that can run this bot, worked out from the blocks in its draft.

builder_version.description:
Which builder built the bot. Only the current one can be written; every version can be
read.

workspace.description:
The workspace the bot belongs to. Absent when it belongs to none. Workspaces are not
managed through this API and are identified by an integer, as they have no uuid.

has_unpublished_changes.description:
Whether the draft differs from what is published. A bot that has never been published
always has changes to publish.

edited_at.description: When the content last changed. Absent on a bot that has never been written to.

BotSummary.description:
A bot as a listing reports it. It is read from the bot's own rows and from nothing else, so
it carries no avatar, no channel and no conversation counters — those belong to other
contexts and are not served here yet.

builder_version.description:
Which builder built the bot. Only the current one can be written; every version is
listed.

edited_at.description: When the content last changed. Absent on a bot that has never been written to.

edited_by.description: Who last changed the content, read from the same side as `edited_at`.

last_published_at.description:
When the bot was last published. Absent until it has been published, and it is what the
default order sorts by.

published_by.description: Who published it last. Absent until the bot has been published.

Author.description:
Someone who did something to a bot. The id is the one the rest of the product identifies a
person by, an integer, since people are not identified by uuid here. The name is the one
every other screen shows for them, and is empty for someone who never filled theirs in.

workspace.description:
The workspace to file the bot under. A workspace that does not exist, or belongs to
another brand, is rejected with `422`.

source.description:
Duplicate an existing bot. Not served yet: on its own it is refused with `501` and
nothing is created. Cannot be combined with `diagram`; sending both is rejected with
`422`.

diagram.description:
The diagram the bot is born with, stored exactly as sent.

Checked before anything else: break a rule and you get `422` with nothing created.
**This is the one place a block we do not describe is refused** rather than stored.

Omit it and the bot starts with a start point and nothing else. Cannot go with `source`.

BotSource.description: The bot to duplicate. Its diagram is copied into the new bot's draft.

BotPatch.description:
What a write to the bot itself may carry. Every field is optional and only the ones sent are
written, so a body carrying none of them is refused rather than answered as a write that
changed nothing. `name`, `workspace` and `is_active` are the bot's own settings; `state` is
which side of the trash it is on, and `active` is its one accepted value.

workspace.description:
The workspace to file the bot under. Send `null` to file it under none. A workspace that
does not exist, or belongs to another brand, is rejected with `422`.

state.description:
Set to `active` to restore a bot from the trash. `trashed` is not accepted: the trash is
entered by deleting the bot.

Diagram.description:
Your diagram, kept as you sent it: keys we do not model — notes, embedded bricks — come back
untouched. The one thing we add is `isTarget: true`, on any node that does
not already say whether a connection may end at it.

We read `nodes` and `connections` to check it. A diagram missing either is stored anyway and
reported as breaking rules.

DiagramNode.description:
One block placed in the diagram, in the builder's own shape. The block is named by
`template`, the storage name; the semantic name a definition carries is the one used to
address blocks in the block-level operations, and the catalog maps between them.

template.description:
Which block this is. Several blocks share a template and are told apart by their params,
which is what a definition's `selector` states.

path.description:
Where the block sits in the diagram's nesting. Equal to `id` at the top level; a block
inside a brick is reached through the brick.

name.description: The label the author gave this block

params.description:
The block's configuration, as described by its definition in the catalog. Validated
against the variant selected by these same params.

top.description: How far down the builder's canvas the block sits

left.description: How far across the builder's canvas the block sits

Connection.description:
One connection, in the builder's own shape. It says which output of which block it leaves
from, and which block it arrives at.

id.description: The key this connection is stored under, repeated inside it.

sourcePath.description: The block the connection leaves from

targetPath.description: The block the connection arrives at

type.description:
Which of the source block's outputs this connection leaves from, exactly as the block
definition's `outputs` report it — some ids carry a `$` prefix and some do not, and the
two are not interchangeable.

has_unpublished_changes.description:
Whether this diagram differs from the one the channels run, so that reading the draft
answers both what is being edited and whether it is still to be published. Same field
and same answer as the bot's.

violations.description:
The business rules the diagram broke on the last write. Empty on a bot that has just been
created, because creating a bot does not validate.

edited_at.description:
When the draft was last written. `null` on a bot whose draft has never been written,
under the convention above for a representation that carries a stored diagram.

DraftWrite.description:
Either a `diagram` to store, or a `source` to take the diagram from — one or the other, not
both. Only the `diagram` branch is served: a body carrying `source` answers `400`, since
`diagram` is required.

oneOf.title: A revision to step back to

DraftSource.description:
An earlier revision of this same draft, to step back to without publishing anything.

A published version is not a source here — bringing one of those back is
`POST /bots/{bot_id}/versions`.

DraftPatch.description:
A set of changes applied together. Describe the diagram you want, not the steps: the whole
result is checked once, and the refusals are judged against it.

**A block id may appear in only one of `add`, `update` and `delete`.** Naming the same block
in two of them contradicts itself and answers `400`, before your draft is read.

update.description: Each entry names the block to change by `id`.

delete.description: Ids of blocks to remove. The connections touching them are removed too and reported.

Each entry names the block a connection leaves from and which of its outputs, so every
stored connection matching it is removed. Naming wiring that is not there is applied
all the same, and removes nothing.

params.description: Replaces the block's params as a whole.

top.description: How far down the builder's canvas to move the block. Omitted, it stays where it is.

left.description: How far across the builder's canvas to move the block. Omitted, it stays where it is.

ConnectionRef.description:
A connection, named by the block it leaves from and which of its outputs. In a diagram the
same two things are `sourcePath` and `type`.

Either can come back empty: a diagram is stored as you sent it, so a connection in it may be
missing one.

connections.description:
Connections to add along with the blocks. They may reference blocks in this request or
blocks already in the diagram.

id.description:
The id to give the block. Generated when omitted. A client that sends connections in
the same request needs to set it.

top.description: How far down the builder's canvas to place the block. Omitted, it is placed at the origin.

left.description: How far across the builder's canvas to place the block. Omitted, it is placed at the origin.

params.description: Replaces the block's params as a whole.

top.description: How far down the builder's canvas to move the block. Omitted, it stays where it is.

left.description: How far across the builder's canvas to move the block. Omitted, it stays where it is.

RuleViolation.description:
One business rule broken by the diagram. The same shape is used wherever violations are
reported: inside a draft, and in a `422` when an operation requires a valid diagram.

code.description:
The rule that was broken, and the thing here safe to branch on.

**[When a call fails](https://dev.landbot.io/api-reference/bots/errors)** lists every code,
says which are refused on the spot and which are stored with the draft, and what each one
is about. A code you get that is not on that list came from a bot an older builder wrote.

message.description:
Human-readable description of what is wrong. One sentence, and it names neither what was
sent nor what would have been accepted: `code` is what identifies the rule, `param` and
`block_id` what it is about, and `GET /blocks` what each rule accepts.

block_id.description:
The block that breaks the rule, for a rule about one block. Inside a draft it comes as
`null` when there is none; inside a `422` it is omitted instead.

param.description:
The param the rule applies to, for a rule about one param. Same as `block_id`: `null`
inside a draft, omitted inside a `422`.

connections.description:
The connections the rule concerns, for rules about wiring — for instance
`connection_output_removed`, where these are the connections left without an output.
Empty for every other rule.

Publication.description:
What a publication did. This is what publishing answers today, in place of the version
resource described below.

publication_count.description: How many times this bot has been published, this publication included.

name.description:
A label, absent unless someone has set one. Versions are created unnamed; naming one is a
separate action.

published_by.description:
Who published it. Absent once that person has left the brand — there is nothing left to
name them by.

allOf.description:
A version together with what it published. It keeps its empty fields rather than omitting
them, for the reason the draft does: it carries a stored diagram, and dropping what has no
value would drop it from inside the diagram too.

channel_version.description:
The channel the bot was served on, as it stood when the version was published. It is
carried verbatim from the context that owns channels and nothing here models it: a
version is shown as it ran, and the diagram alone does not say what the bot looked
like. `null` for a bot whose family has no channel of its own.

VersionCreate.description:
What a publication may be asked for. Sent empty, or not sent at all, it publishes the draft.
Carrying a `source`, it restores the version named there. Nothing else is read: a field this
does not declare is refused naming it, so a caller cannot send a diagram, a label or an
author beside the version and have any of it published.

VersionSource.description:
The publication to bring back. Its diagram is stored in your draft and published from there,
and the greeting a visitor is met with goes back with it.

**The channel's own look does not**: design, style, logo and the rest stay as they are today.
Restoring a flow should not undo brand changes.

name.description:
The block's semantic name. It is what the block-level operations address a block by.

A diagram node names the same block by its `template`, and the catalog does not publish
the template yet, so a client holding a diagram cannot tell from here which definition
describes a node it already has.

can_be_welcome.description:
Whether this block may take the greeting slot. **Check it here** — you cannot work it out
from the block itself. Put any other block in the slot and the diagram breaks
`welcome_block_not_allowed`.

variants.description:
One entry when the block behaves the same way regardless of its params. More than one
when a param changes what the block is: the `selector` says which.

selector.description:
The conditions over a block's own params that select this variant. Empty on a
single-variant block, which any params select.

outputs.description: The fixed outputs a connection can leave from, as used in a connection's `type`.

output_derivations.description:
Rules the caller runs over its own params to know the outputs this variant reports for
them, on top of the fixed `outputs` — a button block reports one output per button.
Empty when every output is fixed.

param_derivations.description:
Params this variant works out itself rather than the caller writing them, and the param
each one is worked out from. What a caller sends for a derived param is replaced or kept
according to the derivation's `kind`. Empty when every param is the caller's. Applied
when a block is added or edited, and not by `PUT /bots/{bot_id}/draft`, which stores what
it is given.

channel_restriction.description: Channel families this variant is valid on. Empty means every one of them.

answer.description:
What kind of answer the block collects, for the blocks that ask for one. Absent on a
block that asks for nothing.

interaction.description:
Whether the block pauses the conversation waiting for the user. This is what makes a
cycle in the diagram legitimate or not: a loop through blocks that never wait is an
error.

ParamDefinition.description:
A param you write. An array declares its element under `item`, an object its `fields`, and a
`one_of` the ways it may be written under `one_of`.

**`read_when` is a condition on another param.** While it does not hold, this param is
ignored: not its rules, not even being required. A block often keeps a value it no longer
reads, and this is how you tell that apart from a value that is wrong.

has_default.description:
Whether a value is applied when the param is absent. It answers what `default` alone
cannot: a param whose default is `null`, `0` or an empty list is not a param without one.

default.description:
The value used when the block is placed and the param is not given. Absent when
`has_default` is false.

item.description: What one element of an array param is. Present only on an array param.

fields.description: The params an object param is made of. Empty on a param that is not an object.

one_of.description:
The shapes this value may take, when it may take more than one — a condition that is
either an object or a bare string, say. Each is a param in its own right.

A value matching none of them is refused with `param_no_matching_shape`. Empty unless
`type` is `one_of`.

read_when.description:
The conditions under which the param is read, written in the same vocabulary as a
variant's `selector` and evaluated the same way. Every one of them has to hold. Empty on
a param that is always read, which is most of them.

ParamElement.description:
What one element of an array is. An element carries a type and the rules every one of them
answers to, and nothing else a param carries: it has no name to be addressed by, it is never
absent, and no default is applied to it. An element of type `one_of` declares each way it may
be written under `one_of`, as a param does.

fields.description: The params an element of type object is made of.

item.description: An element of type array declares its own element here.

one_of.description: The ways this element may be written. Empty unless `type` is `one_of`.

ParamType.description:
The kind of value a param takes. `one_of` is the one that is not a shape of its own: it says
the value may be written in more than one way, and the ways are under `one_of`.

InteractionKind.description:
`waits_for_input` pauses the conversation until the user answers. `runs_without_input` moves
on by itself.

ParamSelector.description:
One condition to evaluate over your own params. `match` says which:

- `equals` — the param carries `value`. `matches_null` says whether a null counts.
- `has_items` — the param is a list with something in it.
- `any_item_matches` / `every_item_matches` — read `field` inside each item of a list. An
  empty list satisfies `every_item_matches`.

matches_null.description:
Whether a param with no value satisfies this condition. That is how an absent param can
still select a variant.

value.description: The value to compare against. Absent for a condition that compares none.

field.description:
The field read inside each item, for `any_item_matches` and `every_item_matches`. Absent
for the conditions that compare the param itself.

OutputDerivation.description:
Run this over your own params to know the outputs a block has: one per item of the `param`
list, with the id `id_prefix` + the item's `id_field`. An item whose `id_field` is empty gives
no output. Derived outputs come before the fixed ones.

**A derived id must start with `$`.** One that does not is refused with
`param_output_id_invalid` and nothing is stored.

param.description: The array param whose items become outputs.

id_field.description:
The field of an item that carries the output's id. Declared under the `fields` of the
param's `item`, so what it carries can be read there.

id_prefix.description: What the derived id starts with.

title_field.description: The field of an item that carries the output's title, when it has one.

ParamDerivation.description:
A param we work out for you from another one. `kind` says what happens to a value you send
for it: `compiled_formula` replaces it with what `source` compiles to; `rendered_text` keeps
it, and works it out from `source` only when you send none.

Applied when a block is added or edited, not on a whole-diagram write. A `source` that will
not compile is refused with `param_formula_not_compiled`.

kind.description:
Which derivation this is: `compiled_formula` compiles a formula into the tree the runtime
reads, and `rendered_text` writes a plain text as the HTML the widget renders.

source.description: The param it is derived from, which the caller does write.

name.description:
Which constraint this is. A caller can enforce the same rule before writing, and gets the
same code back in a violation if it does not.

constraint.description:
The rule's own value, where it takes one: the maximum length, the regular expression the
value matches or the one it must not carry, the values allowed, the values reserved, the
functions a formula may call. Absent for a rule that takes none, as `non_empty` and
`json` do.

id.description:
The value to use as a connection's `type`, verbatim, `$` prefix included where the
definition carries one.

code.description:
A stable identifier for the failure, suitable for branching on. Each refusal names
itself, and so does a failure of a service this API depends on.

message.description: A short description of what went wrong.

name.description: The field the problem is in.

examples: name must be at most 50 characters

allOf.description:
The draft, as answered by an operation that can drop wiring the caller did not name. Only
those operations answer this shape; the ones that add or edit a block answer a plain
`Draft`, having nothing to remove.

removed_connections.description:
The wiring that was in the draft and is no longer there. Always sent, and empty when
nothing was removed. Reported so that no wiring disappears without the caller being
told. What removes it depends on the operation: `DELETE
/bots/{bot_id}/draft/blocks/{block_id}` reports what went with the block, and `PATCH
/bots/{bot_id}/draft` reports that and the connections the change set deleted by name,
each one listed once.

ConnectedAccount.description: A Google account somebody connected to the brand, as much of it as a block needs to name it.

name.description:
The Google account's email as it read when it was connected, unless somebody renamed the
account in the app.

id.description: The file as Google Drive identifies it, which is what a block's `spreadsheet_id` takes.

The tab's own id. Not compiled: the editor keeps it as `sheet_id` and nothing reads it
when the bot runs.

index.description: The column's number counting from 1, which is what `selectorValue` takes.

ConnectionStarted.description: A connection just opened, and where a person goes to answer it.

url.description:
Where a member of the brand goes, in a browser signed in to the app, to connect the
account. Nothing a token does on its own.

allOf.description: When the link stops working, fifteen minutes after it was started.

AccountConnection.description: A connection as it stands when read.

status.description:
`pending` until the person answers, then `connected` or `declined` for good; `expired`
once fifteen minutes pass unanswered.

account_id.description:
The account the person connected, which is what a block's `auth_id` takes. `null` in
every status but `connected`.

ErrorResponse.description:
A failure carrying a code to branch on. It is what every refusal this API names answers
with: a bot or a version that cannot be read, a bot or a draft that cannot be written, and a
depended-on service that fails.

ErrorMessageResponse.description:
A failure carrying only a message, which is how a request this API does not serve yet is
answered. There is nothing to branch on, so the status code is the whole of the news.

examples: Duplicating a bot is not available yet

DetailErrorResponse.description:
A refusal decided before the request reaches this API: credentials, permission, the method,
the rate. It carries `detail` rather than `error`, and there is nothing in it to branch on —
the status is the whole of the news.

FieldErrorsResponse.description:
A body that could not be read: a field missing, or carrying the wrong type. Each key is the
field at fault and its value the reasons, and the envelope carries neither `error` nor a code.

InputErrorResponse.description:
The house shape for malformed input, kept as the target for `400`. Not answered yet: today a
malformed body comes back as `FieldErrorsResponse`.

violations.description: The rules broken, when they can be attributed to specific blocks or params.
